stem: A team evaluates a summarization model by comparing its summaries with human-written reference summaries, measuring how many words and phrases overlap.
prompt: Which metric is commonly used for this?

options.text: BLEU
options.why: BLEU also measures n-gram overlap with references, but it is precision-oriented and was designed for machine translation, not summarization.

options.text: ROUGE
options.why: ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) measures word and phrase overlap with reference summaries and is the standard summarization metric.

options.text: BERTScore
options.why: BERTScore compares meaning using embeddings rather than counting overlapping words and phrases.

options.text: Perplexity
options.why: Perplexity measures how well a model predicts text and needs no reference summary, so it does not compare against human-written summaries.

explanation.answer: ROUGE evaluates automatic summarization (and other generation) by measuring overlap between generated text and reference texts, for example ROUGE-1 (unigrams), ROUGE-2 (bigrams) and ROUGE-L (longest common subsequence). It is recall-oriented.
explanation.concept: Overlap metrics are cheap and automatic but miss meaning when wording differs; semantic metrics such as BERTScore and LLM-as-a-judge address that.
explanation.examTip: Summarization overlap metric = ROUGE.

stem: A localization team evaluates a model's machine translations by comparing them with professional human translations, focusing on how precisely the n-grams match.
prompt: Which metric is traditionally used for this?

options.text: Perplexity of an image model
options.why: This is not a translation evaluation metric.

options.text: Mean absolute error
options.why: MAE measures numeric error, not text similarity.

options.text: BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy)
options.why: BLEU is a precision-oriented n-gram overlap metric originally designed for evaluating machine translation.

options.text: F1 score for fraud
options.why: F1 evaluates classification, not translation quality.

explanation.answer: BLEU measures how closely machine-generated text matches reference translations based on n-gram precision, with a brevity penalty. It is the classic metric for machine translation.
explanation.concept: BLEU (precision-oriented, translation) and ROUGE (recall-oriented, summarization) both rely on word overlap and can undervalue valid paraphrases.
explanation.examTip: Translation overlap metric = BLEU. Summarization = ROUGE.

stem: A team finds that ROUGE gives low scores to generated answers that use different wording from the references but mean the same thing. It wants a metric that compares meaning rather than exact words.
prompt: Which metric fits?

options.text: Accuracy on a classification test set
options.why: Classification accuracy does not measure similarity of free text.

options.text: Latency
options.why: Latency measures how fast a response arrives, not whether it means the same thing as the reference.

options.text: BLEU
options.why: BLEU also relies on exact n-gram overlap, so it has the same weakness.

options.text: BERTScore
options.why: BERTScore compares contextual embeddings of tokens in the generated and reference texts, capturing semantic similarity beyond exact word overlap.

explanation.answer: BERTScore uses contextual embeddings from a pre-trained model to compute similarity between generated and reference texts, rewarding paraphrases that preserve meaning. It complements overlap metrics such as ROUGE and BLEU.
explanation.concept: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation reports metrics such as BERTScore for some task types and offers LLM-as-a-judge for qualities such as correctness and helpfulness.
explanation.examTip: Meaning-based similarity using embeddings = BERTScore.

references.title: Evaluate the performance of Amazon Bedrock resources

stem: A team needs to evaluate thousands of chatbot responses for helpfulness, correctness and tone. Human review of all of them is too slow and expensive.
prompt: Which approach scales evaluation while approximating human judgment?

options.text: LLM-as-a-judge scoring responses against a rubric
options.why: An evaluator model can assess helpfulness, correctness and tone at scale, with human spot checks to calibrate it.

options.text: BERTScore against reference answers
options.why: BERTScore needs a reference answer for every response and measures similarity, not helpfulness or tone.

options.text: ROUGE against reference answers
options.why: ROUGE counts word overlap with references, which says little about helpfulness or tone.

options.text: Human review of a 1% random sample
options.why: Sampling keeps costs down but covers only a small fraction of the responses; it does not scale evaluation to all of them.

explanation.answer: LLM-as-a-judge uses a capable model to score or compare outputs against rubrics, such as correctness, completeness, helpfulness, harmfulness and style. Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation supports LLM-as-a-judge with built-in and custom metrics.
explanation.concept: Judge models have biases too; validate them against human ratings on a sample, and keep humans in the loop for high-stakes decisions.
explanation.examTip: Scale quality evaluation with a judge model = LLM-as-a-judge.

stem: A company is choosing a model to write empathetic responses to customers who have experienced a bereavement. Automated metrics do not capture whether responses feel appropriate and compassionate.
prompt: Which evaluation approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: LLM-as-a-judge with an empathy rubric
options.why: A judge model scales well, but it is still an automated method, and for such a sensitive use case trained people should judge compassion.

options.text: Human evaluation by trained reviewers
options.why: Subjective, high-stakes qualities such as empathy and appropriateness are best judged by trained people using clear guidelines.

options.text: BERTScore against reference condolence messages
options.why: Semantic similarity to a reference does not show whether a response feels compassionate to the reader.

options.text: Toxicity scores from automatic evaluation
options.why: Low toxicity shows a response is not harmful, not that it is empathetic and appropriate.

explanation.answer: Human evaluation captures nuanced, subjective qualities, such as empathy, tone, cultural appropriateness and brand fit, that automatic metrics miss. Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation supports human evaluation jobs using your own workforce or an AWS-managed team.
explanation.concept: Combine human evaluation (depth) with automatic metrics and LLM-as-a-judge (scale).
explanation.examTip: Subjective qualities (empathy, tone) → human evaluation.

references.title: Evaluate the performance of Amazon Bedrock resources

stem: A team wants a managed AWS capability to compare several foundation models on its own prompt dataset, using automatic metrics, LLM-as-a-judge and optional human reviewers, without building an evaluation pipeline itself.
prompt: Which capability should the team use?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
options.why: Guardrails filter content in production; they do not run evaluation jobs comparing models on a dataset.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management
options.why: Prompt Management compares prompt variants, but it does not run automatic, judge-based and human evaluation jobs across models.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation
options.why: Bedrock Model Evaluation runs managed evaluation jobs with automatic metrics, LLM-as-a-judge and human reviewers on your own datasets.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
options.why: Model Monitor tracks deployed models for drift over time; it does not compare candidate foundation models.

explanation.answer: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation provides managed evaluation of models and RAG systems: automatic evaluation with metrics (such as accuracy, robustness and toxicity) on curated or custom datasets, LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, and human evaluation.
explanation.concept: Evaluation is needed for model selection, prompt changes, fine-tuning decisions and ongoing monitoring.
explanation.examTip: Managed model comparison on your data = Bedrock Model Evaluation.

references.title: Evaluate the performance of Amazon Bedrock resources

stem: A team reads that a model scores highly on a well-known public benchmark for question answering. It wonders whether the model will perform as well on its insurance-claims questions.
prompt: Which statement is MOST accurate?

options.text: A score above 90% predicts similar results on its claims questions
options.why: Benchmarks cover particular tasks and data; performance on a specialized domain can differ significantly.

options.text: Benchmarks measure speed and cost, not answer quality
options.why: Most benchmarks measure task performance, so this misdescribes them.

options.text: Benchmarks are unreliable, so rely on user feedback only
options.why: Benchmarks are a useful starting point; user feedback alone comes too late to choose a model.

options.text: Benchmarks help shortlist; validate on the team's own claims questions
options.why: Benchmarks give a standardized starting point, but only representative data from the use case shows real performance.

explanation.answer: Benchmark datasets provide standardized comparisons across models, but they may not represent your domain, and models may have seen benchmark data during training. Always evaluate on representative data from your use case.
explanation.concept: Bedrock Model Evaluation lets you bring custom prompt datasets alongside built-in ones.
explanation.examTip: Benchmarks = starting point. Your own data = deciding factor.

stem: A RAG assistant gives poor answers. The team needs to know whether the problem is that relevant passages are not being retrieved, or that the model writes bad answers even from good passages.
prompt: Which evaluation approach separates these issues?

options.text: Evaluate retrieval relevance separately from answer faithfulness
options.why: Measuring each stage separately shows whether retrieval or generation is the weak link.

options.text: Score end-to-end answer correctness with an LLM judge
options.why: End-to-end scores show answers are poor but not whether retrieval or generation caused it.

options.text: Collect user thumbs-up and thumbs-down ratings on answers
options.why: User ratings reveal dissatisfaction, not which stage of the pipeline is failing.

options.text: Compare answers to reference answers using BLEU
options.why: BLEU measures overlap of the final answer only, so it cannot separate retrieval problems from generation problems.

explanation.answer: RAG applications should be evaluated at two levels: retrieval quality (are the retrieved chunks relevant and do they cover the needed information?) and generation quality (is the answer correct, complete and faithful to the retrieved context?). Amazon Bedrock offers RAG evaluation for knowledge bases with retrieve-only and retrieve-and-generate modes.
explanation.concept: Faithfulness (groundedness) checks that answers do not add information beyond the sources.
explanation.examTip: RAG evaluation = retrieval metrics + generation metrics, separately.

stem: A team evaluates an agent that books meetings. Its individual responses read well, but the team is unsure whether meetings are actually booked correctly.
prompt: Which evaluation focus is MOST important for this agent?

options.text: ROUGE of the agent's replies against reference replies
options.why: Text overlap shows how replies are worded, not whether meetings were actually booked correctly.

options.text: Task completion and whether the right tools got the right parameters
options.why: For agents, success means completing the task correctly, so evaluation must check actions and tool calls.

options.text: User ratings of how polite and clear the replies are
options.why: Polite, clear replies can still accompany a booking that failed or was made for the wrong time.

options.text: Average latency and tokens per conversation
options.why: Speed and cost matter, but they do not show whether bookings are correct.

explanation.answer: Evaluating agents focuses on outcomes and behavior: task completion rate, correctness of actions, tool selection and parameter accuracy, number of steps, errors and recovery, safety of actions, and cost per task. Trace-based evaluation examines each step.
explanation.concept: Workflows and agents need end-to-end evaluation in addition to evaluation of individual model outputs.
explanation.examTip: Agents are judged on task completion and correct tool use.

stem: An executive asks how to judge whether a customer-service AI assistant is meeting business objectives, not just producing good-sounding text.
prompt: Which metrics BEST align with business objectives?

options.text: ROUGE and BERTScore on sampled conversations
options.why: These measure text similarity to references, not whether customers' issues are resolved at an acceptable cost.

options.text: Average latency and tokens per response
options.why: These are operational metrics; they do not show resolution or satisfaction.

options.text: Task completion rate, user satisfaction and cost per interaction
options.why: These measure whether issues get resolved, whether customers are satisfied, and at what cost, which ties the assistant to business value.

options.text: Toxicity and robustness scores from model evaluation
options.why: These are important safety and quality checks, but they do not show business impact.

explanation.answer: Business objective alignment metrics for AI applications include task completion rate, user satisfaction (CSAT), cost per interaction, deflection or containment rate, time saved and conversion. These tie model behavior to business value.
explanation.concept: Track technical metrics for quality and business metrics for value; both are needed.
explanation.examTip: Business alignment = task completion, satisfaction, cost per interaction.

stem: A company deployed an AI writing assistant for its marketing staff. It wants to know whether the FM is effectively meeting the business objective of making the team more productive.
prompt: Which measurement BEST answers this?

options.text: BERTScore of drafts against the team's past content
options.why: Similarity to past content says nothing about whether the team now works faster.

options.text: Number of drafts generated per user each week
options.why: Usage shows adoption, not whether approved content gets produced faster.

options.text: LLM-judge quality scores for the generated drafts
options.why: Draft quality matters, but the objective is productivity, which needs time and output measured against a baseline.

options.text: Time to approved content and output volume, before and after
options.why: Comparing productivity before and after adoption directly measures whether the FM meets the business objective.

explanation.answer: To determine whether an FM meets business objectives, measure outcomes such as productivity (time saved, throughput), user engagement (adoption, retention, acceptance of suggestions) and quality of the final work, ideally against a baseline.
explanation.concept: The exam guide lists productivity, user engagement and task engineering as ways to judge FM effectiveness against business goals.
explanation.examTip: Is it helping the business? Measure productivity and engagement against a baseline.

stem: A team matches evaluation metrics to tasks.
prompt: Which pairings are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Image generation → mean absolute error on token counts
options.why: This is not a meaningful image generation metric.

options.text: Machine translation → BLEU
options.why: BLEU was designed to evaluate machine translation against references.

options.text: House price prediction → BLEU
options.why: Price prediction is regression and uses metrics such as RMSE.

options.text: Text summarization → ROUGE
options.why: ROUGE is a standard summarization metric based on overlap with references.

options.text: Fraud classification → ROUGE
options.why: Fraud classification uses precision, recall, F1 or AUC.

explanation.answer: Choose metrics that fit the task: BLEU for translation, ROUGE for summarization, BERTScore for semantic similarity, LLM-as-a-judge or human ratings for open-ended quality, and classic metrics (accuracy, F1, RMSE) for traditional ML tasks.
explanation.concept: No single metric captures everything; combine automatic metrics with human or judge-model assessment.
explanation.examTip: BLEU = translation. ROUGE = summarization. BERTScore = semantic similarity.

stem: A RAG answer states a fact that is true in the real world but does not appear anywhere in the retrieved documents.
prompt: Which RAG evaluation dimension flags this?

options.text: Faithfulness (groundedness) to the retrieved context
options.why: Faithfulness checks whether every claim is supported by the provided context, regardless of real-world truth.

options.text: Answer correctness against a reference answer
options.why: The fact is true, so it could still score as correct; correctness does not check whether the answer came from the sources.

options.text: Context relevance of the retrieved passages
options.why: Relevance scores the retrieved passages, not whether the answer added information beyond them.

options.text: Context coverage of the retrieval results
options.why: Coverage measures whether retrieval found the needed information, not whether the answer stayed within it.

explanation.answer: Faithfulness, also called groundedness, measures whether every claim in an answer is supported by the retrieved context. Ungrounded claims are a risk even when they happen to be true, because the system is supposed to answer from approved sources.
explanation.concept: Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding checks and Bedrock RAG evaluation both assess grounding.
explanation.examTip: Answer contains info not in sources → low faithfulness / groundedness.

stem: A team wants to check automatically whether a model's answers stay accurate when prompts contain small typos or rephrasings, and whether it produces toxic content.
prompt: Which evaluation dimensions are these?

options.text: Parameter count and context window
options.why: These describe the model, not its behavior.

options.text: Robustness and toxicity
options.why: Robustness measures stability under small input changes, and toxicity measures harmful content.

options.text: Latency and throughput
options.why: These are performance measures, not quality or safety dimensions.

options.text: Cost and storage
options.why: These are financial and infrastructure measures.

explanation.answer: Automatic model evaluation in Amazon Bedrock includes dimensions such as accuracy, robustness (how outputs change with small semantic-preserving perturbations to inputs) and toxicity (presence of harmful content), using built-in or custom datasets.
explanation.concept: Robustness and safety evaluations are part of responsible AI practice.
explanation.examTip: Stable under typos = robustness. Harmful content = toxicity.

stem: A team frequently updates prompts and switches models. Sometimes a change that improves one type of question quietly breaks another.
prompt: Which practice BEST catches these regressions?

options.text: Spot-check the question type each change targets
options.why: Testing only the targeted cases misses regressions in other question types, which is exactly the problem.

options.text: Monitor user ratings in production after each change
options.why: Production feedback detects regressions only after users have been affected.

options.text: Rerun a representative golden dataset on every change
options.why: A fixed, representative test set evaluated before each deployment reveals regressions across all question types.

options.text: Use an LLM judge on outputs for the changed questions only
options.why: Judging only the changed questions does not catch breakage elsewhere.

explanation.answer: A golden evaluation dataset, covering representative and edge-case inputs with expected outcomes or rubrics, enables regression testing of prompts, models and RAG configurations. Automating evaluation in the release process (an MLOps practice) prevents silent quality drops.
explanation.concept: Combine automatic metrics, LLM-as-a-judge and human review on sampled cases.
explanation.examTip: Catch regressions → rerun a golden evaluation set on every change.

stem: A document-processing workflow has four steps: extract fields, classify the document, summarize it and route it. End-to-end accuracy is 70%, and the team does not know which step causes failures.
prompt: Which evaluation approach is MOST useful?

options.text: Measure end-to-end accuracy on a larger test set
options.why: A larger test set gives a more precise 70%, but still does not show which step fails.

options.text: Score the final routed documents with an LLM judge
options.why: Judging only the final output shows the outcome, not where errors originate.

options.text: Evaluate only the summarization step, the most complex one
options.why: Assuming the cause skips the other three steps, any of which could be failing.

options.text: Evaluate each step with its own metrics, plus end to end
options.why: Step-level metrics show which step drives failures, while end-to-end metrics measure overall success.

explanation.answer: Applications built from multiple FM steps (workflows, RAG, agents) should be evaluated component by component and end to end. Component metrics localize problems; end-to-end metrics measure the business outcome.
explanation.concept: Errors compound across steps: four steps at 92% each give about 72% end to end.
explanation.examTip: Multi-step app → evaluate each step + the whole.

stem: Offline evaluations show that a new prompt version is better. The team wants to confirm its real-world impact on customer satisfaction before rolling it out to everyone.
prompt: Which approach BEST confirms this?

options.text: A/B test with part of real traffic on the new version
options.why: An A/B test measures real customer outcomes, such as satisfaction and task completion, against a control group.

options.text: Rerun the offline evaluation with a larger test set
options.why: More offline data improves the estimate but still does not measure real customer satisfaction.

options.text: Roll out to everyone, then compare with last month's scores
options.why: Before-and-after comparisons are confounded by other changes over time, and everyone is exposed at once.

options.text: Have an LLM judge rate both versions on past chats
options.why: This is still an offline evaluation; it does not measure real customers' satisfaction.

explanation.answer: Offline evaluation estimates quality; online evaluation, such as A/B tests or canary releases, confirms real-world impact on business metrics like satisfaction, completion and conversion.
explanation.concept: Collect user feedback (thumbs up/down, ratings) to support ongoing evaluation.
explanation.examTip: Confirm real impact → A/B test with real traffic.

stem: A team relies entirely on an LLM judge to score answers. They notice the judge consistently prefers longer answers, even when shorter ones are more accurate.
prompt: What should the team do?

options.text: Switch to a larger judge model and keep the same rubric
options.why: Larger judges can share the same length bias; the rubric and calibration are what need fixing.

options.text: Calibrate the judge against human ratings and penalize needless length
options.why: Comparing the judge with human ratings and refining the rubric corrects known biases, with periodic human review to confirm.

options.text: Replace the judge with ROUGE against reference answers
options.why: ROUGE cannot assess open-ended qualities the judge was chosen for and has its own length effects.

options.text: Ask the judge to explain its reasoning before scoring
options.why: Explanations can help, but they do not by themselves remove a systematic preference for longer answers.

explanation.answer: LLM-as-a-judge is scalable but can show biases such as preferring longer or more confident answers or favoring certain styles. Clear rubrics, calibration against human labels and periodic human audits keep evaluations trustworthy.
explanation.concept: Human-in-the-loop evaluation remains the reference standard for subjective quality.
explanation.examTip: LLM judges have biases → rubric + human calibration.

stem: A company's FM performs well on individual questions, but employees still spend a long time because the AI step does not fit how their work is actually organized.
prompt: Which consideration does this highlight when judging whether an FM meets business objectives?

options.text: Model capability: the FM needs to be more accurate
options.why: The FM already performs well on individual questions, so accuracy is not the gap.

options.text: Latency: the responses need to arrive faster
options.why: The delay comes from how the AI step fits the work, not from response speed.

options.text: Task engineering: fitting the AI into how the work is done
options.why: Business value depends on integrating the model into the real task flow so it removes work instead of adding steps.

options.text: Cost: the per-token price is too high
options.why: Cost is not the issue described; employees are slowed by the workflow.

explanation.answer: Determining whether an FM meets business objectives includes task engineering: designing how the model fits into the end-to-end task so that it saves effort, plus measuring productivity and engagement. Good outputs alone do not guarantee business value.
explanation.concept: Measure end-to-end time and outcomes, gather user feedback, and redesign the workflow around the AI where needed.
explanation.examTip: Great outputs but no time saved → fix task/workflow integration.

stem: A team wants to evaluate open-ended creative answers for which no single correct reference text exists.
prompt: Which evaluation method is MOST suitable?

options.text: BERTScore against one example answer
options.why: With many valid creative answers, similarity to a single example would penalize good answers that differ from it.

options.text: BLEU against a single reference answer
options.why: Overlap with one reference penalizes valid creative variation.

options.text: Perplexity of each answer under the model
options.why: Perplexity measures how predictable text is to a model, not whether an answer is good.

options.text: Rubric-based scoring by an LLM judge and human reviewers
options.why: Rubric-based judging assesses relevance, coherence and creativity without needing a reference answer.

explanation.answer: Reference-based metrics (ROUGE, BLEU, BERTScore) need ground-truth text. For open-ended or creative tasks, rubric-based evaluation by human reviewers or LLM judges (assessing relevance, coherence, creativity, safety) is more appropriate.
explanation.concept: Choose evaluation methods according to whether reliable reference answers exist.
explanation.examTip: No reference answer → rubric-based human or LLM-judge evaluation.

stem: A team built a knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock and wants managed evaluation of both its retrieval results and the generated answers, including metrics such as correctness, completeness and faithfulness.
prompt: Which capability should the team use?

options.text: RAG evaluation in Amazon Bedrock Evaluations
options.why: Bedrock evaluates knowledge bases in retrieve-only and retrieve-and-generate modes, with metrics such as correctness, completeness and faithfulness.

options.text: Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding checks
options.why: Grounding checks filter individual responses at runtime; they do not evaluate retrieval quality across a test set.

options.text: SageMaker Model Monitor for the knowledge base
options.why: Model Monitor tracks drift for SageMaker endpoints; it does not evaluate Bedrock knowledge base retrieval and answers.

options.text: Bedrock model invocation logging
options.why: Logging records requests and responses but does not score them.

explanation.answer: Amazon Bedrock Evaluations supports evaluating RAG applications built with Bedrock Knowledge Bases (or your own RAG system). Retrieve-only evaluations measure context relevance and coverage; retrieve-and-generate evaluations measure qualities such as correctness, completeness, faithfulness and responsible-AI metrics.
explanation.concept: Use these evaluations to tune chunking, retrieval settings, prompts and models.
explanation.examTip: Managed RAG quality evaluation = Bedrock Evaluations for knowledge bases.

stem: A company launches an AI assistant that answers customer billing questions.
prompt: Which metrics BEST show alignment with business objectives? (Select TWO.)

options.text: BERTScore of answers against reference answers
options.why: Similarity to reference answers is a technical quality metric; it does not show business impact.

options.text: Percentage of billing questions resolved without a human agent
options.why: Resolution without escalation measures task completion and cost savings.

options.text: Average response latency in milliseconds
options.why: Latency is an operational metric. It affects experience but does not show whether billing issues are resolved.

options.text: Customer satisfaction ratings after assistant conversations
options.why: Satisfaction shows whether the experience meets customer needs.

options.text: Toxicity score from automatic model evaluation
options.why: Toxicity is a safety check, not a measure of business value.

explanation.answer: Business alignment metrics for AI applications include task completion or resolution rate, user satisfaction, cost per interaction, average handle time and escalation rate.
explanation.concept: Pair them with quality and safety metrics so cost savings do not come at the expense of correctness.
explanation.examTip: Resolution rate + satisfaction + cost per interaction = business alignment.

stem: A regulated bank is about to launch a generative AI assistant for internal staff and needs an evaluation strategy that is thorough, scalable and defensible to auditors.
prompt: Which strategy is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Use a public benchmark score and the provider's model card
options.why: These describe the model in general, not its behavior on the bank's tasks, so they are not defensible evidence for this use.

options.text: Layer automatic, judge and expert review; document it and monitor
options.why: Combining automatic metrics, LLM-as-a-judge and human expert review balances scale and depth; documentation and monitoring satisfy auditors.

options.text: Have human experts review every response before launch
options.why: Reviewing every response is thorough but does not scale, and launch-time review alone misses issues that appear later.

options.text: Run LLM-as-a-judge on a large test set and launch if it passes
options.why: This scales, but without expert review of high-risk cases, documentation or monitoring it is not defensible to auditors.

explanation.answer: Robust FM evaluation combines several approaches: automatic metrics, LLM-as-a-judge at scale, human-in-the-loop review for nuance and risk, task-specific and adversarial test sets, and post-deployment monitoring, all documented for governance.
explanation.concept: Evaluation evidence can be recorded in model documentation such as SageMaker Model Cards to support audits.
explanation.examTip: Defensible evaluation = automatic + judge + human + documentation + monitoring.
